idiom_name: nested step interfaces + one sealed Steps class + explicit interface implementation + static Create()
implementation_notes: C# has exactly the primitives the pattern needs - nested interfaces, explicit interface implementations (so the intermediate methods stay out of IntelliSense), a private constructor and a static entry point - but nothing in the language stages the calls, so the chain is hand-written: one interface per step, one sealed class implementing them all, and Build() on the final interface only. Since C# 11 the required modifier plus init-only setters make a single object initializer enforce that every required member is set, which replaces staging when only presence matters; combine both when a few members are mandatory and many are optional, and reserve the staged chain for a real sequence. Builders are single-use mutable accumulators: keep them local to one expression.
pitfalls: Implementing the step members implicitly (public methods) re-exposes every setter on every stage; explicit interface implementation is what keeps the intermediate calls off the intermediate types.

A constructor marked [SetsRequiredMembers] overrides the compiler's required-member check entirely - the annotation is an assertion, not a guarantee, so a stale or wrong constructor silently removes the safety net.
The builder mutates its own fields: sharing one instance between threads (or caching it in a static) interleaves accumulations, and partial state from a failed chain stays behind.
